readings.title: The Red Badge of Courage: the tattered man’s questions (Chapter X)
readings.challenge: Follow how a kind man’s questions become, in Henry’s mind, an attack, and judge what Henry does about them.
readings.focus: Shame turns concern into a threat, and Henry abandons a wounded man to keep his secret.
readings.context: Stephen Crane’s The Red Badge of Courage (1895) follows Henry Fleming, called “the youth,” a Union volunteer, through two days of a Civil War battle. Recap: in his first fight Henry stood and helped drive back one charge, then ran from the second. Wandering behind the lines, he joined a column of wounded men, where a tattered soldier, hit in the head and the arm, kept asking him where he was hurt; Henry has no wound. Among the wounded he found his friend Jim Conklin, the tall soldier, and watched him die in a field. A “jim-dandy” is a fine fellow; “peek-ed” means pale and sickly; “swad” means a crowd. The dialect spellings are Crane’s.
readings.contentNote: These war-fiction excerpts contain battlefield violence, death, injury and profanity. The narrative critically examines heroic expectations and a frightened soldier’s self-justifications. This chapter describes the body of a soldier who has just died and a badly wounded man left wandering alone in a field; at its end Henry wishes he were dead, which the novel presents as the unstable reasoning of shame, not as advice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, the whole chapter; opens “The tattered man stood musing.”; closes “…could not defend himself against this agency. It was not within the power of vigilance.”.

questions.prompt: The tattered man tells two stories about wounds: Tom Jamison telling him he was shot, and the man hit in the head who “didn't feel nothin'.” What does he mean the stories to do for Henry, and why do they do the opposite?
facilitatorNotes: He means them kindly: wounds can be worse than they seem, so Henry should “watch out” and take care of his. Both stories are about hurts a man cannot see in himself, which is exactly the subject Henry dreads, because his hurt is shame, not a wound. Each friendly question about where it is “located” presses on the lie.
evidence: Yeh might have some queer kind 'a hurt yerself.
Where is your'n located?

questions.prompt: By the end the tattered man calls Henry “Tom Jamison” and begs him not to go “trompin' off—with a bad hurt.” What is happening to him, and what does Henry recognize before he climbs the fence?
facilitatorNotes: His wits are failing; Henry sees that he, “like that other one,” is beginning to act “dumb and animal-like,” as Jim Conklin did before dying. Henry knows the man may be dying and leaves him anyway. The confused plea fits Henry painfully well: he is the one going off with a hurt he will not show. Readers can argue whether the tattered man is simply delirious or still trying to look after someone.
evidence: like that other one, was beginning to act dumb and animal-like
Turning at a distance he saw the tattered man wandering about helplessly in the field.

questions.prompt: The narrator says the questions “asserted a society that probes pitilessly at secrets until all is apparent.” Is this the narrator’s judgment or Henry’s? Is it fair to the tattered man?
facilitatorNotes: The sentence reports Henry’s feeling in the narrator’s grand vocabulary, and the grandness is ironic: the questions were “simple,” and the man asking them was dying and kind. Still, Henry is not wholly wrong that a community will ask, and that a secret like his cannot be kept by vigilance alone. A strong answer separates the truth in his fear from the unfairness of turning it on this man.
evidence: The simple questions of the tattered man had been knife thrusts to him.
They asserted a society that probes pitilessly at secrets until all is apparent.

readings.title: The Red Badge of Courage: hoping for a defeat (Chapter XI)
readings.challenge: Follow Henry’s argument with himself step by step, and notice where the narrator’s wording undercuts it.
readings.focus: Heroic daydreams, practical excuses, and the secret wish that the army will lose so that running will look like good sense.
readings.context: Recap: after watching Jim Conklin die, Henry abandoned the tattered soldier, who was himself wounded and confused and kept asking where Henry was hurt. Alone, Henry comes out on the road behind the battle. Teamsters drive the supply wagons; a malediction is a curse; a cowled man wears a monk’s hood; “the colors” are a regiment’s flags; craven means cowardly and a loon here is a fool. Laurels and crowns are traditional honours for the heroic dead.
readings.contentNote: These war-fiction excerpts contain battlefield violence, death, injury and profanity. The narrative critically examines heroic expectations and a frightened soldier’s self-justifications. Henry again wishes he were dead and imagines corpses on the field; the passage presents this as the unstable reasoning of shame, not as advice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, the whole chapter; opens “He became aware that the furnace roar of the battle was growing louder. Great brown…”; closes “…remark in a low tone. At it the others all crowed and cackled. He was a slang phrase.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the sight of the fleeing wagons comfort Henry, while the column marching forward makes his “woe” return?
facilitatorNotes: The wagons are “all retreating,” so his own flight looks ordinary; he even magnifies their terror to prove to himself that running was sensible. The column going to the front looks like “a procession of chosen beings,” and he feels he can never be one of them. Each sight matters to him only as a judgment on himself.
evidence: They were all retreating. Perhaps, then, he was not so bad after all.
He felt that he was regarding a procession of chosen beings.

questions.prompt: Henry pictures himself “getting calmly killed on a high place before the eyes of all.” What stops him from going to the front: the objections, his body, or something in the daydream itself?
facilitatorNotes: All three work together. The objections are practical (no rifle, no regiment) until the real one appears: someone would ask him for “an explanation.” His thirst, aching bones and dizziness finish the plan. But the daydream was always a scene played “before the eyes of all,” and the same fear of being looked at that feeds it also kills it. The narrator’s mock-solemn “very formidable” lets us smile at how easily he gives in.
evidence: getting calmly killed on a high place before the eyes of all
he could not but admit that the objections were very formidable

questions.prompt: Henry argues that a defeat would prove he “had fled early because of his superior powers of perception.” How does Crane make this sound clever and absurd at once? Where does Henry see through it, and does that last?
facilitatorNotes: The prophet who climbs a tree before the flood is a neat image, but it turns running into wisdom and treats the general who would be blamed as “of no consequence.” Henry then calls himself the “most unutterably selfish man in existence” and the murderer of the soldiers who would die, yet a few paragraphs later he is inventing “a fine tale” for his regiment. Some readers see a real conscience struggling; others see one more mood in a mind that turns everything toward itself.
evidence: A serious prophet upon predicting a flood should be the first man to climb a tree.
He said that he was the most unutterably selfish man in existence.

questions.prompt: The chapter ends: “He was a slang phrase.” What does Henry fear most by the end, and what does this reveal about the kind of courage he has been dreaming of?
facilitatorNotes: He fears the regiment’s stares and jokes (“He run, didn't 'e?”) more than wounds or death: to become a joke is to be reduced to a phrase. His idea of courage has been about reputation, how he looks to others, rather than about what he does. Readers may connect this to his earlier wish for a wound to show.
evidence: Where's Henry Fleming? He run, didn't 'e? Oh, my!
He was a slang phrase.

readings.title: The Red Badge of Courage: the wound (Chapter XII)
readings.challenge: Notice the irony in how Henry gets his wound, and how little he can see or understand for most of the chapter.
readings.focus: The “red badge” arrives by accident from his own side, and a stranger’s kindness brings him home.
readings.context: Recap: behind the lines Henry imagined heroic charges, then hoped the army would lose so that his running would look like foresight; deciding that defeat was impossible, he tried and failed to invent a story to take back to his regiment. A plank road was surfaced with wooden planks; a squadron of cavalry is a unit of soldiers on horseback; facings are the coloured trim of a uniform; fishwives sold fish and were known for loud scolding; provost-guards are military police. “Johnnies” is Union slang for Confederate soldiers.
readings.contentNote: These war-fiction excerpts contain battlefield violence, death, injury and profanity. The narrative critically examines heroic expectations and a frightened soldier’s self-justifications. This chapter includes a blow to the head, the reported death of a soldier shot in the head, and a mention of amputation.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, the whole chapter; opens “The column that had butted stoutly at the obstacles in the roadway was barely out of the…”; closes “…out of his life, it suddenly occurred to the youth that he had not once seen his face.”.

questions.prompt: How does Henry get his wound? Why is the way it happens ironic in a book called The Red Badge of Courage?
facilitatorNotes: A fleeing Union soldier clubs him with his rifle when Henry clutches his arm to ask what has happened. The wound comes from his own side, in a rout, while he is asking a question, not fighting. Earlier Henry wished for a wound that would certify his courage; now he has a real one that proves nothing of the kind.
evidence: stammered the youth struggling with his balking tongue
He adroitly and fiercely swung his rifle. It crushed upon the youth's head.

questions.prompt: In Chapter XI Henry hoped for a defeat. When the beaten men come rushing at him, what happens to that hope?
facilitatorNotes: He is “horrorstricken”; he throws aside his “mental pamphlets on the philosophy of the retreated.” The defeat he imagined as a private excuse arrives as terror and chaos, and the grand speech he wants to make shrinks to “what 's th' matter?” Crane shows how thin the earlier reasoning was once the real thing appears.
evidence: He threw aside his mental pamphlets on the philosophy of the retreated and rules for the guidance of the damned.
but he could only get his tongue to call into the air

questions.prompt: The cheery soldier talks for a whole page, finds the way “with a strange fortune,” and leaves before Henry sees his face. Why does Crane make Henry’s rescuer faceless and nameless?
facilitatorNotes: He is the opposite of the tattered man: he asks questions and answers them himself, wanting nothing back. His story of Jack, killed while a stranger kept pestering him for the road, echoes Henry pestering the fleeing soldier. A rescuer without a face does good unseen, unlike the heroism Henry imagines, which needs “the eyes of all.” Some readers find him almost magical (a “wand”); others see the ordinary decency that war also contains.
evidence: seemed to the youth to possess a wand of a magic kind
it suddenly occurred to the youth that he had not once seen his face

readings.title: The Red Badge of Courage: a story told by the fire (Chapter XIII)
readings.challenge: Compare the story Henry tells with what you know happened, and watch how others finish the story for him.
readings.focus: A wound taken as proof, and a boastful friend who has become a gentle one.
readings.context: Recap: as the Union line broke, a fleeing soldier struck Henry on the head with his rifle when Henry seized his arm. Dazed, he was led through the dark woods by a cheerful stranger, who brought him to his regiment’s campfire and left before Henry saw his face. Wilson, “the loud soldier,” was a boastful private in Henry’s company before the battle. A corporal commands a handful of men; a sentinel is a guard on watch; “het up” means heated.
readings.contentNote: These war-fiction excerpts contain battlefield violence, death, injury and profanity. The narrative critically examines heroic expectations and a frightened soldier’s self-justifications.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIII, the whole chapter; opens “The youth went slowly toward the fire indicated by his departed friend. As he reeled, he…”; closes “…gave a long sigh, snuggled down into his blanket, and in a moment was like his comrades.”.

questions.prompt: Compare the tale Henry tells Wilson with what happened. Which words are true, which are false, and which are neither?
facilitatorNotes: He did have “an awful time,” he was separated from the regiment, and he was hurt in the head. “Over on th' right” and “Ter'ble fightin'” are invented, and “I got shot” is false. The narrator has just said he had “no strength to invent a tale,” so the story is half confusion and half calculation; readers can decide how much is lying and how much is exhaustion.
evidence: Over on th' right, I got shot. In th' head.
He had no strength to invent a tale; he would be a soft target.

questions.prompt: How do Wilson and the corporal complete Henry’s lie for him? Who, in the end, gives it authority?
facilitatorNotes: Wilson cuts in before Henry can say more (“he got shot in th' head”), and the corporal examines the wound and calls it a graze “by a ball.” The community’s own experts certify the story. Yet the corporal’s comparison, a lump “as if some feller had lammed yeh on th' head with a club,” states the truth without knowing it.
evidence: Yes, an' he got shot in th' head an' he's in a fix
It's raised a queer lump jest as if some feller had lammed yeh on th' head with a club.

questions.prompt: Wilson was “the loud soldier” before the battle. What has changed in him, and why does Henry try to stop him at the end?
facilitatorNotes: He is now a fussing “amateur nurse” who gives his coffee, his handkerchief and finally his own blanket, and snaps at Henry for objecting. Henry’s “I've got your———” shows he has realized whose blanket it is. The kindness falls on a lie: Henry is cared for as a wounded hero. Readers may ask whether his gratitude includes guilt, and whether Wilson’s change came from what the battle taught him.
evidence: He had the bustling ways of an amateur nurse.
I've got your———

readings.title: The Red Badge of Courage: morning, and a changed friend (Chapter XIV)
readings.challenge: Watch how Henry measures the change in his friend, and what his own words show about whether he has changed.
readings.focus: Wilson’s new modesty set against Henry’s need to score a point, on the morning of the second day.
readings.context: Stephen Crane’s The Red Badge of Courage (1895) follows Henry Fleming, called “the youth,” a Union volunteer, through two days of a Civil War battle. Recap: on the first day Henry ran from the second Confederate charge. Wandering behind the lines, he watched his friend Jim Conklin die, and was then struck on the head by a fleeing Union soldier. Back at his regiment’s fire that night he let everyone believe the wound came from a bullet, and his friend Wilson, once “the loud soldier,” nursed him and gave him his own blanket. A charnel place is a house for the dead; “the rebs” are the Confederates; “the hull kit-an'-boodle” means the whole lot; pacific means peace-making.
readings.contentNote: These war-fiction excerpts contain battlefield violence, death, injury and profanity. The narrative critically examines heroic expectations and a frightened soldier’s self-justifications.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIV, the whole chapter; opens “When the youth awoke it seemed to him that he had been asleep for a thousand years, and…”; closes “"So?" said the youth.”.

questions.prompt: Waking, Henry takes the sleeping men for corpses, then decides the picture is “a mere prophecy.” What does the opening suggest about the day to come, and about the state of Henry’s mind?
facilitatorNotes: The dawn light gives the men “corpselike hues,” and the narrator’s word “prophecy” warns that many of these sleepers will be dead by evening. It also shows a mind still disordered by the blow and the night before: for an instant he believes he is “in the house of the dead.” Readers can decide whether the prophecy is Henry’s or the narrator’s.
evidence: He believed for an instant that he was in the house of the dead
He saw that this somber picture was not a fact of the present, but a mere prophecy.

questions.prompt: List the changes Henry notices in Wilson. When Henry reminds him of his old boasting, how does Wilson answer, and what does the reminder show about Henry?
facilitatorNotes: Wilson no longer measures “his personal prowess,” is not stung by small words, and has “a fine reliance.” Henry’s jab about licking “the hull kit-an'-boodle” is the kind of point-scoring Wilson has given up, and Wilson simply agrees (“perhaps I would”). Henry is left “disconcerted” and backs away. The exchange suggests that Henry still lives by comparison with others, as Wilson used to.
evidence: He was no more a loud young soldier. There was about him now a fine reliance.
"Well, perhaps I would," he decided at last. He stared humbly at the fire.

questions.prompt: Henry mentions Jim Conklin’s death only when “a sudden thought came to him” in the middle of an argument. What does the timing of the news suggest about Henry, and about how war treats a death?
facilitatorNotes: He has carried the memory all night but produces it as a point in a dispute about who saw more of the fight. Some readers will see callousness; others, shock that has not yet let the death become real. Wilson’s short reply (“poor cuss!”) and the immediate quarrel at the next fire show how quickly the camp moves on.
evidence: Then a sudden thought came to him. "Oh! Jim Conklin's dead."
Jim Conklin. . . . poor cuss!

questions.prompt: The chapter ends with Wilson’s remark that the lost men came back from “wanderin' around in th' woods... Jest like you done,” and Henry’s one word, “So?” What might Henry be thinking, and why might Crane end the chapter here?
facilitatorNotes: Wilson innocently gives Henry cover: so many men drifted back that one more absence means nothing. But “Jest like you done” puts Henry beside men who were “fightin' with other reg'ments,” which he was not. His “So?” is guarded: relief, caution and guilt are all possible, and Crane leaves the reader to supply them.
evidence: They'd been scattered all over, wanderin' around in th' woods, fightin' with other reg'ments, an' everything. Jest like you done.
"So?" said the youth.

readings.title: The Red Badge of Courage: the packet of letters (Chapter XV)
readings.challenge: Separate what Henry believes about himself from what the narrator lets you see, sentence by sentence.
readings.focus: A secret kept as a weapon, and a self-image rebuilt because no one found out.
readings.context: Recap: on the second morning Henry, whose comrades believe his head wound came from a bullet, found his friend Wilson changed from a braggart into a quiet peacemaker. Before the first battle Wilson, sure he would be killed, gave Henry a packet of letters in a yellow envelope to send to his family. “Order arms” is a position with the rifle butt on the ground; lugubrious means mournful; laurels are a traditional crown of honour; to rail is to complain bitterly. The “young lady at the seminary” is a girl at the school where Henry said goodbye to his schoolmates before leaving home.
readings.contentNote: These war-fiction excerpts contain battlefield violence, death, injury and profanity. The narrative critically examines heroic expectations and a frightened soldier’s self-justifications.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, the whole chapter; opens “The regiment was standing at order arms at the side of a lane, waiting for the command to…”; closes “…ones doing brave deeds on the field of battle without risk of life would be destroyed.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Henry decide not to mention the packet, and what does he think he gains by keeping it?
facilitatorNotes: The packet records Wilson’s fear in his own hand, so it is “a small weapon” Henry can use if Wilson ever asks what Henry did yesterday. Holding back is not kindness but strategy: “He was master.” Ask what it means that Henry’s first thought about a friend’s confession is how to use it.
evidence: He now rejoiced in the possession of a small weapon with which he could prostrate his comrade at the first signs of a cross-examination.
He was master.

questions.prompt: “He had performed his mistakes in the dark, so he was still a man.” What idea of manhood is Henry working from? How does the narrator’s wording show what he thinks of it?
facilitatorNotes: For Henry, what no one saw does not count: manhood is reputation. The narrator lets him speak in grand terms (“the chosen of gods and doomed to greatness”) and then deflates him with phrases like “fled with discretion and dignity,” which no one could say seriously. Some readers find Henry contemptible here; others find him painfully ordinary.
evidence: He had performed his mistakes in the dark, so he was still a man.
As for himself, he had fled with discretion and dignity.

questions.prompt: When Wilson asks for the letters back, Henry gives them up and “took unto himself considerable credit.” Was his silence generous? Compare who feels shame in this scene with who has more to be ashamed of.
facilitatorNotes: He stayed silent only because he “could conjure nothing of sufficient point.” Wilson blushes over a moment of fear that he confessed honestly, while Henry, who ran and lied, feels himself “an individual of extraordinary virtues.” Crane’s irony is plain, but a reader may note that Henry did, in the end, spare his friend.
evidence: He could conjure nothing of sufficient point.
he was an individual of extraordinary virtues

questions.prompt: Henry decides that only “the doomed and the damned” complain about the universe, then imagines telling war stories at home. How do these two thoughts belong together?
facilitatorNotes: Both come from comfort: with “a full stomach and the respect of his fellows,” he sees no reason to question anything, and the same complacency lets him picture himself as “the central figure in blazing scenes.” A day earlier he raged at the universe; now he feels secure because his secret is safe. Readers can judge whether any of this confidence has been earned.
evidence: Let the unfortunates rail; the others may play marbles.
He saw his gaping audience picturing him as the central figure in blazing scenes.

readings.title: The Red Badge of Courage: blaming the general (Chapter XVI)
readings.challenge: Follow an argument about who is to blame for defeat, and notice which remarks make Henry go quiet.
readings.focus: Retreat, rumour and complaint: talk fills the time before the next attack.
readings.context: Recap: Henry, whose comrades think his head wound came from a bullet, returned his friend Wilson’s packet of letters without a word and congratulated himself on his generosity; he now feels sure no one will discover that he ran. The regiment moves up to the front. A rifle pit is a shallow trench; skirmishers and pickets are soldiers posted ahead of the main line; the Rappahannock is a river in Virginia; a lunkhead is a blockhead; “from pillar to post” means pushed from place to place; “chin music” is idle talk.
readings.contentNote: These war-fiction excerpts contain battlefield violence, death, injury and profanity. The narrative critically examines heroic expectations and a frightened soldier’s self-justifications.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVI, the whole chapter; opens “A sputtering of musketry was always to be heard. Later, the cannon had entered the…”; closes “…stood awaiting the shock. Some shrank and flinched. They stood as men tied to stakes.”.

questions.prompt: Henry wants to joke “All quiet on the Rappahannock,” but cannot finish the sentence. How does Crane use sound in the opening paragraphs, and what happens to the rumours when the guns stop?
facilitatorNotes: The guns are “engaged in a stupendous wrangle,” so loud that “it became impossible to make a sentence heard”; the joke itself, a newspaper phrase for a quiet front, is defeated by the noise it mocks. When the guns stop, rumours fly “like birds,” but black ones that flap “near to the ground,” and the men read omens in them. The soundscape carries the regiment’s mood.
evidence: It became impossible to make a sentence heard.
they were now for the most part black creatures who flapped their wings drearily near to the ground

questions.prompt: Henry blames the general; Wilson blames luck. Whose explanation is better supported, and why does Henry feel “secretly dumfounded” at his own words?
facilitatorNotes: Henry argues that if the regiment fights “like the devil” and still loses, the general must be at fault; Wilson, “in a weary tone,” allows that the general “did th' best he knowed.” Neither has evidence, but Henry’s argument depends on a “we” that includes himself, and he knows he did not fight. Readers may decide whether Wilson’s modesty or Henry’s anger is closer to the truth.
evidence: "Well, don't we fight like the devil? Don't we do all that men can?" demanded the youth loudly.
He was secretly dumfounded at this sentiment when it came from his lips.

questions.prompt: Why does the sarcastic man’s remark reduce Henry to “an abject pulp,” though the man means nothing by it? How is Henry’s new modesty different from Wilson’s?
facilitatorNotes: “Mebbe yeh think yeh fit th' hull battle” touches the real secret by chance. Henry goes quiet out of fear of exposure: he becomes “suddenly a modest person” in order not to be noticed. Wilson’s modesty in Chapter XIV came from knowing himself better; Henry’s is protective camouflage.
evidence: Mebbe yeh think yeh fit th' hull battle yestirday, Fleming
He became suddenly a modest person.

questions.prompt: The lieutenant tells the men to stop arguing, then adds one more complaint of his own. What is funny about his outburst, and how does the last paragraph change the tone?
facilitatorNotes: He orders silence while venting “his inward dissatisfaction” himself, and his parting line about “too much chin music” is more chin music. Then the comedy stops: exhausted men wait for the attack “as men tied to stakes,” an image of helpless victims rather than heroes. The shift prepares for the fury of the next chapter.
evidence: There's too much chin music an' too little fightin' in this war, anyhow
They stood as men tied to stakes.

readings.title: The Red Badge of Courage: a war devil (Chapter XVII)
readings.challenge: Trace how Henry’s grievance becomes rage, and how others see him when the fighting stops.
readings.focus: Courage without thought: Henry fights like an animal and then decides he is a hero.
readings.context: Stephen Crane’s The Red Badge of Courage (1895) follows Henry Fleming, called “the youth,” a Union volunteer, through two days of a Civil War battle. Recap: Henry ran from his first battle and returned with a head wound that his comrades believe came from a bullet. On the second morning his regiment was pulled back through the woods while he complained bitterly about the generals; now the Confederates attack again. To be “at bay” is to be cornered and forced to turn and fight; a ramrod pushes the charge down a rifle barrel; a “piler men” is a pile of men.
readings.contentNote: These war-fiction excerpts contain battlefield violence, death, injury and profanity. The narrative critically examines heroic expectations and a frightened soldier’s self-justifications. The chapter describes Henry’s fantasies of cruelty and revenge, and the soldiers chant an old rhyme approving the beating of dogs and women; both are presented as the bravado of exhausted men, not endorsed.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVII, the whole chapter; opens “This advance of the enemy had seemed to the youth like a ruthless hunting. He began to…”; closes “…smoldering ruins, went up toward the sun now bright and gay in the blue, enameled sky.”.

questions.prompt: At the start of the chapter, why does the enemy’s attack make Henry furious rather than afraid? Trace the steps of his reasoning.
facilitatorNotes: He feels he has “earned opportunities for contemplative repose” after yesterday’s “adventures” (his flight, renamed), so the attack seems a personal insult. Yesterday he hated the universe; today he hates the enemy “with the same great hatred.” Some readers will see the first real courage in this; others will see wounded pride finding a new target.
evidence: For to-day he felt that he had earned opportunities for contemplative repose.
He was not going to be badgered of his life, like a kitten chased by boys, he said.

questions.prompt: Find the animal comparisons in the fighting. What do they suggest about the kind of courage Henry shows here?
facilitatorNotes: A “cur-like snarl,” animals “tossed for a death struggle into a dark pit,” a line that writhes “like a snake stepped upon,” and Henry going forward “like a dog.” His bravery is instinct, not choice: he does not know he is standing and keeps firing when there is nothing to shoot at. Crane neither glorifies it nor dismisses it.
evidence: his teeth set in a cur-like snarl
To the youth the fighters resembled animals tossed for a death struggle into a dark pit.

questions.prompt: “He had slept and, awakening, found himself a knight.” How does Henry interpret what has happened? Which words suggest the narrator is less impressed than Henry is?
facilitatorNotes: Henry first sees that he was “a barbarian, a beast,” then quickly turns this into heroism. The narrator’s “no doubt” and “what he called a hero” keep a distance, and a comrade has just called him an “infernal fool.” The men look at him “as a war devil,” which is awe mixed with alarm. Readers may still credit Henry with real courage, earned without his knowing it.
evidence: He had been a tremendous figure, no doubt.
and he was now what he called a hero

questions.prompt: The men celebrate with an old rhyme and a joke about sweeping up the dead, and the chapter closes on smoke “as from smoldering ruins” under a “gay” sky. How do these endings pull against each other?
facilitatorNotes: The rhyme claims that beating improves things, and the men apply it to their battered regiment; the dustpan joke reduces the enemy dead to sweepings. The final image sets ruin against a bright, indifferent sky, as nature in this novel often ignores the fighting. The men’s cheer and the narrator’s image do not agree, and readers can decide which has the last word.
evidence: Th' more yeh beat 'em, th' better they be!
A cloud of dark smoke, as from smoldering ruins, went up toward the sun now bright and gay in the blue, enameled sky.

readings.title: The Red Badge of Courage: “mule drivers” (Chapter XVIII)
readings.challenge: Listen to two officers talk about Henry’s regiment, and judge what Henry learns from overhearing them.
readings.focus: Seen from above, a regiment is a tool; Henry discovers that he is insignificant.
readings.context: Recap: in the morning’s fighting Henry, who ran on the first day, fought in a blind fury and was hailed by his lieutenant as a “wild cat”; he decided he was a hero. Jimmie Rogers is the soldier Wilson stopped from fighting that morning. A division is a large body of several brigades, each made up of regiments; a cavalcade is a group of riders. Mule drivers drove the army’s supply wagons and were thought of as rough labourers, not soldiers.
readings.contentNote: These war-fiction excerpts contain battlefield violence, death, injury and profanity. The narrative critically examines heroic expectations and a frightened soldier’s self-justifications. A soldier shot through the body screams and curses his comrades.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVIII, the whole chapter; opens “The ragged line had respite for some minutes, but during its pause the struggle in the…”; closes “…assent when a shaggy man near them said in a meek voice: "We'll git swallowed."”.

questions.prompt: Why do the men hesitate before going to Jimmie Rogers, and how does he answer their hesitation? Why might Crane give his wound so little space?
facilitatorNotes: They stop “as if they feared to go near,” as if death might be catching, and Rogers answers with “a tremendous, fantastic contempt.” The next paragraph moves straight on to the search for water: in battle one man’s agony has no room, even when it is the man whose quarrel Wilson settled that morning. Readers may find the brevity cold or truthful.
evidence: When their eyes first encountered him there was a sudden halt, as if they feared to go near.
he damned them in shrieked sentences

questions.prompt: How do the general and the officer talk about sending the regiment forward? Find the words that show their tone.
facilitatorNotes: The general speaks “coolly, as if he were criticising his clothes,” and the officer chooses the regiment because it is the one he “can spare.” The general’s last remark is sober but unmoved, and the officer smiles. Readers can consider whether a commander could think any other way and still do his job.
evidence: spoke coolly, as if he were criticising his clothes
I don't believe many of your mule drivers will get back.

questions.prompt: “New eyes were given to him.” What does Henry learn from the overheard order? Is it the same lesson Wilson seems to have learned in Chapter XIV?
facilitatorNotes: He learns he is “very insignificant”: the regiment is a broom to sweep some part of the woods. Wilson’s humility seemed to grow from within; Henry’s is handed to him from outside, and he finds it only “strange.” Some readers will say both men are learning the same truth by different roads; others, that Henry has not yet accepted it.
evidence: New eyes were given to him.
The officer spoke of the regiment as if he referred to a broom.

questions.prompt: Why don’t Henry and Wilson tell the others what they heard? What does their nod at “We'll git swallowed” show about them now?
facilitatorNotes: Telling would only frighten the men, and the secret is also a kind of private knowledge, “an ironical secret.” Their nod shows a new steadiness: they will go forward knowing the odds, with “no hesitation in each other's faces.” Readers may argue that the men deserved to know.
evidence: It was an ironical secret.
they nodded a mute and unprotesting assent

readings.title: The Red Badge of Courage: the charge and the flag (Chapter XIX)
readings.challenge: Follow a charge that starts, stalls and starts again, and notice what moves the men each time.
readings.focus: A frenzy that forgets the self, and a flag that becomes an idol and then a dead man’s burden.
readings.context: Recap: fetching water, Henry and Wilson overheard their division’s general choose their regiment for a charge because its men “fight like a lot 'a mule drivers,” and say that few would come back; they kept it to themselves. The colors are a regiment’s flag, carried by a color sergeant; men rally to it, and losing it disgraces a regiment. A battery is a group of cannon; imprecations are curses.
readings.contentNote: These war-fiction excerpts contain battlefield violence, death, injury and profanity. The narrative critically examines heroic expectations and a frightened soldier’s self-justifications. Men are killed and maimed in the charge, a dead soldier’s body is pulled from the flag he carried, and the narrator compares the shouting men to “tortured savages,” a dated and demeaning image.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIX, the whole chapter; opens “The youth stared at the land in front of him. Its foliages now seemed to veil powers and…”; closes “…high, and the curved hand fell with heavy protest on the friend's unheeding shoulder.”.

questions.prompt: In the open field Henry seems to see “everything.” What does he see clearly, and what can he never explain afterward?
facilitatorNotes: Every blade of grass, the bark of the trees, men falling “to queer, heaped-up corpses”: his mind takes “a mechanical but firm impression.” What it cannot record is his own motive: everything was explained to him later “save why he himself was there.” Ask why such sharp seeing goes with so little understanding.
evidence: It seemed to the youth that he saw everything.
save why he himself was there

questions.prompt: The narrator calls the frenzy of the charge “a temporary but sublime absence of selfishness.” Is this praise? How does the next paragraph test it?
facilitatorNotes: For Henry, whose every thought has been about himself, losing the self is a real change, and “sublime” is strong. But it is also “delirium,” “moblike and barbaric,” and it lasts only while breath does: then the men “returned to caution” and “were become men again.” Readers can argue whether selflessness in a crowd is admirable or simply blind.
evidence: It is a temporary but sublime absence of selfishness.
They were become men again.

questions.prompt: When the charge stalls, what gets the regiment moving: the lieutenant’s curses, Wilson’s shot, or Henry’s anger at the lieutenant? Trace the chain.
facilitatorNotes: The lieutenant’s cursing does not move them; Wilson’s “angry shot” wakes them to their weapons; and at the second halt Henry, furious at being grabbed, answers “Come on yerself, then” and runs out before the colors. Each push comes from anger rather than principle. The narrator’s comparison of the three to “tortured savages” makes the scene look wild rather than noble.
evidence: This action awakened the men.
The private felt a sudden unspeakable indignation against his officer.

questions.prompt: How does Henry see the flag as he runs? Why does Crane follow this vision at once with the struggle over the color sergeant’s body?
facilitatorNotes: The flag becomes a goddess and a woman, beautiful and unhurtable, almost “a saver of lives.” Then the man carrying it is shot, and the corpse seems to tug “in ludicrous and awful ways” for the flag. Idealism meets bodily fact; the dead hand that falls on Wilson’s shoulder reads like a last protest. Readers can decide whether the vision is foolish or what makes the charge possible.
evidence: It was a goddess, radiant, that bended its form with an imperious gesture to him.
the corpse would not relinquish its trust

readings.title: The Red Badge of Courage: a march of shame (Chapter XX)
readings.challenge: Track how Henry’s feeling shifts from shame to fury to pride during the retreat, and find what in the fighting causes each shift.
readings.focus: A failed charge becomes a march of shame, and a short, almost accidental victory gives the men back their belief in themselves.
readings.context: Stephen Crane’s The Red Badge of Courage (1895) follows Henry Fleming, called “the youth,” a Union volunteer, through two days of a Civil War battle. Recap: the regiment charged across a clearing; when the color sergeant was killed, Henry and his friend Wilson wrenched the flag from the dead man’s hands, and Henry kept it. Earlier the general had called the regiment “mule drivers,” and Henry has been dreaming of making him regret it. The colors are the regiment’s flag; Union soldiers wear blue and Confederate soldiers gray, and a facing is the colored trim on a uniform. Crane writes “illusions” where he means allusions.
readings.contentNote: These war-fiction excerpts contain battlefield violence, death, injury and profanity. The narrative critically examines heroic expectations and a frightened soldier’s self-justifications. Wounded men are left behind in the retreat, officers curse, and the dead lie “thrown and twisted into fantastic shapes.”

excerpt.locator: Chapter XX, the whole chapter; opens “When the two youths turned with the flag they saw that much of the regiment had crumbled…”; closes “…new trust in the grim, always confident weapons in their hands. And they were men.”.

questions.prompt: How does Crane show the regiment coming apart during the retreat? Find two things individual men do.
facilitatorNotes: The men act “as if stunned,” glower at their officers as if betrayed, and some slip “with speed back to the lines”; one soldier sinks down and buries his face “with an air of bowing to a doom,” and the wounded are “left crying on this black journey.” The image of “a machine run down” sums it up: the regiment has no force left. Ask what single detail makes the scene most real.
evidence: But the regiment was a machine run down.
Wounded men were left crying on this black journey.

questions.prompt: Why is the retreat “a march of shame” to Henry in particular? What has he lost?
facilitatorNotes: His revenge: he meant to prove the general wrong about the “mule drivers,” and the retreat seems to prove him right. His anger turns ugly; he thinks the officer “would be finer as a dead man.” Readers can discuss whether Henry’s rage is really aimed at the general or at the regiment’s, and his own, failure.
evidence: And now the retreat of the mule drivers was a march of shame to him.
would be finer as a dead man, he thought

questions.prompt: Wilson says, “Well, Henry, I guess this is good-by—John.” Why does Henry answer so harshly?
facilitatorNotes: Wilson expects them to die, and Henry refuses to hear it said; he “would not look at the other.” He has just taken up “the attitude of the color bearer in the fight of the preceding day,” as if stepping into a role, and his hand trembles and he is “choking.” The harshness may be fear held down, or a refusal to give up. Both readings fit the evidence.
evidence: Oh, shut up, you damned fool!
He unconsciously assumed the attitude of the color bearer in the fight of the preceding day.

questions.prompt: The chapter ends “And they were men.” What has the “small duel” really proved? Is the narrator sincere?
facilitatorNotes: The gray regiment was surprised: it “had been unaware of the proximity” of the blue troops, and the lieutenant happened to see it first. Even so, the men learn that “the proportions were not impossible” and dance for joy. The flat last sentence can be read as earnest (they have recovered their nerve) or as gently ironic (their manhood depends on how the last few minutes went). Ask readers to defend one reading from the paragraph before it.
evidence: the small duel had showed them that the proportions were not impossible
And they were men.

readings.title: The Red Badge of Courage: mud diggers, and a jimhickey (Chapter XXI)
readings.challenge: Notice that the same charge is measured three ways: by the ground Henry sees, by the general’s anger, and by the colonel’s praise.
readings.focus: The regiment’s honor rises and falls on what others say about it, and Henry is glad to believe whatever flatters him.
readings.context: Recap: retreating after a failed charge, the regiment was nearly surrounded in the smoke; then the lieutenant spotted a gray regiment close by, and a short, fierce exchange drove it off and gave the men back their pride. Henry still carries the flag. The “officer who had named them as mule drivers” is the general; MacChesnay is the regiment’s colonel and Hasbrouck the lieutenant. A diversion is an attack meant to draw the enemy’s attention from another part of the field; “jimhickey,” like “jim-dandy,” is slang praise.
readings.contentNote: These war-fiction excerpts contain battlefield violence, death, injury and profanity. The narrative critically examines heroic expectations and a frightened soldier’s self-justifications. Officers curse and mock one another; in the retelling, the two friends were “howlin' like Indians,” a period comparison that uses Native Americans as a byword for wildness.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXI, the whole chapter; opens “Presently they knew that no firing threatened them. All ways seemed once more opened to…”; closes “…their hearts swelled with grateful affection for the colonel and the youthful lieutenant.”.

questions.prompt: What do the resting veterans shout as the regiment comes back? Why do the taunts sting so much?
facilitatorNotes: “Where th' hell yeh been?” “Was it warm out there, sonny?” “Goin' home now, boys?” They treat the regiment as raw boys who ran. The men feel it as a public verdict; they trudge “as if they bore upon their bended shoulders the coffin of their honor.” Ask why a stranger’s mockery weighs more than the danger did.
evidence: Was it warm out there, sonny?
the coffin of their honor

questions.prompt: When Henry looks back over the ground they charged across, what astonishes him? What happens to that discovery a paragraph later?
facilitatorNotes: The distances are “trivial and ridiculous,” the trees “incredibly near,” the time short: his mind had enlarged everything. For a moment he grants “bitter justice” in the veterans’ jeers. Then he turns to “considerable joy in musing upon his performances,” and the humbling thought is gone. Readers can discuss whether Henry learns anything here or simply moves on.
evidence: were trivial and ridiculous
Elfin thoughts must have exaggerated and enlarged everything, he said.

questions.prompt: The general says the regiment stopped “about a hundred feet this side of a very pretty success.” How do the colonel, the lieutenant and the men each respond?
facilitatorNotes: The colonel first looks injured, like “a deacon” accused of stealing, then shrugs “like a Frenchman”: “we went as far as we could.” The lieutenant openly calls any such critic “a damned fool,” and the colonel silences him. The men become “like cuffed and cursed animals, but withal rebellious.” The general judges by a plan the men never knew about (a diversion); readers can argue whether he is unfair or simply right about the result.
evidence: Oh, well, general, we went as far as we could
if he says th' boys didn't put up a good fight out there he's a damned fool

questions.prompt: Thompson’s report of the colonel’s praise ends the chapter. How do Henry and Wilson react, and how does Crane want us to take their happiness?
facilitatorNotes: Aloud they scoff (“Yer lyin', Thompson”), but their faces flush “from thrills of pleasure.” Then: “The past held no pictures of error and disappointment.” Henry’s past holds plenty, including his flight and the tattered man; praise lets him forget it. The chapter shows the men’s worth set entirely from outside, first by contempt and then by praise. Some readers find the joy touching rather than ironic; ask for evidence either way.
evidence: they knew that their faces were deeply flushing from thrills of pleasure
The past held no pictures of error and disappointment.

readings.title: The Red Badge of Courage: a spectator with the colors (Chapter XXII)
readings.challenge: Follow Henry as he watches the wider battle like a spectator, then judge the plan he forms when his own regiment is attacked.
readings.focus: Seen from a distance, battle looks like a game or a drama; close up it is wounds, and Henry’s courage feeds on a grudge.
readings.context: Recap: back at their own lines, the regiment was jeered by veterans and scolded by the general, who called the men “mud diggers” for stopping short; then word came that the colonel and the lieutenant had named Henry and Wilson the best fighters in the regiment, and the two were secretly delighted. Henry still carries the flag, so he does not fire. A battery is a group of cannon; “celerity” is speed; “gibelike” means mocking.
readings.contentNote: These war-fiction excerpts contain battlefield violence, death, injury and profanity. The narrative critically examines heroic expectations and a frightened soldier’s self-justifications. A sergeant is shot through the cheeks and the wound is described closely; men fall and lie “twisted into impossible shapes”; Henry imagines his own corpse as a reproach to the general, which the novel presents as the logic of a grudge, not as an ideal.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXII, the whole chapter; opens “When the woods again began to pour forth the dark-hued masses of the enemy the youth felt…”; closes “…The robust voice, that had come strangely from the thin ranks, was growing rapidly weak.”.

questions.prompt: Before his regiment is attacked, Henry watches other parts of the battle. Find two comparisons Crane uses for what he sees. What do they have in common?
facilitatorNotes: Two pairs of regiments slug each other “as if at a matched game” and “as if upon a wager”; a brigade comes out of a wood “airily” and seems to “point a proud thumb”; fences and trees are fought over “as gold thrones or pearl bedsteads.” From outside, war looks like sport or play, its purposes invisible. Ask what the comparisons leave out.
evidence: slugging each other as if at a matched game
as gold thrones or pearl bedsteads

questions.prompt: Henry is “deeply absorbed as a spectator.” How has carrying the flag changed what he does in the fight?
facilitatorNotes: He cannot fire, yet he does not “feel his idleness”: he leans forward at “the great drama,” prattles, and forgets he is breathing. On the first day he panicked and ran; now he is too absorbed to be afraid. Readers may see this as a kind of calm courage or as another way of not quite being there.
evidence: He was deeply absorbed as a spectator.
The crash and swing of the great drama made him lean forward

questions.prompt: What is Henry’s “final and absolute revenge”? What does it show about what drives him now?
facilitatorNotes: His dead body, “torn and gluttering,” would be “a great and salt reproach” to the officer who called them “mule drivers” and “mud diggers.” He resolves not to budge, and the motive is a grudge and a wish to be proved right, even posthumously. Students can argue whether this is bravery, vanity, or both.
evidence: his final and absolute revenge was to be achieved by his dead body lying, torn and gluttering, upon the field
his corpse would be for those eyes a great and salt reproach

questions.prompt: Why might Crane place the orderly sergeant’s wound right after Henry’s revenge fantasy?
facilitatorNotes: Henry imagines a meaningful corpse; the sergeant shows a real body, his jaw hanging and his mouth “a pulsing mass of blood and teeth,” trying to shriek “as if he conceived that one great shriek would make him well.” The idea of a death that sends a message meets a wound that means nothing. “The regiment bled extravagantly” keeps the scene from becoming heroic.
evidence: as if he conceived that one great shriek would make him well
The regiment bled extravagantly.

readings.title: The Red Badge of Courage: the fence, the flag and four prisoners (Chapter XXIII)
readings.challenge: Read a charge from inside Henry’s excitement, then notice how the four prisoners afterward give the enemy separate faces.
readings.focus: The craving for the enemy’s flag turns the men into a mob, and then four captured men in gray become individuals.
readings.context: Stephen Crane’s The Red Badge of Courage (1895) follows Henry Fleming, called “the youth,” a Union volunteer, through two days of a Civil War battle. Recap: on the second day of the battle Henry carries his regiment’s flag, and he and his friend Wilson have just heard that their colonel praised them. Now gray soldiers behind a rail fence are cutting down the thinned regiment, which cannot stay where it is. A color bearer carries a regiment’s flag, and taking an enemy’s colors was one of the proudest things a regiment could do. “Obdurate” means stubborn; “consigned them to red regions” means told them to go to hell.
readings.contentNote: These war-fiction excerpts contain battlefield violence, death, injury and profanity. The narrative critically examines heroic expectations and a frightened soldier’s self-justifications. An enemy color bearer dies clutching his flag; Crane compares Henry’s frenzy to the spirit of “a savage religion mad,” an image of fanaticism; a prisoner curses his captors.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXIII, the whole chapter; opens “The colonel came running along back of the line. There were other officers following him.…”; closes “…with vanity, came to him there. They sat side by side and congratulated each other.”.

questions.prompt: Henry expects that the tired men will have to be driven to charge. What happens instead, and how does the narrator explain it?
facilitatorNotes: They give “quick and unqualified expressions of assent” and race forward. The narrator does not call it reasoned courage: it is “a paroxysm,” the strength “that comes before a final feebleness,” a frenzy “perhaps because of forgotten vanities,” with “no obvious questioning, nor figurings, nor diagrams.” Ask whether that explanation makes the charge less admirable.
evidence: A knowledge of its faded and jaded condition made the charge appear like a paroxysm
There was no obvious questioning, nor figurings, nor diagrams.

questions.prompt: What does the enemy flag become in Henry’s mind? Trace the comparisons.
facilitatorNotes: “A craved treasure of mythology, hung amid tasks and contrivances of danger”: a quest prize. He plunges at it “like a mad horse,” and the two flags meet like eagles with “strange beaks and claws.” The language of legend makes a killing ground into an adventure. Readers can compare it with the flag as a goddess in the earlier charge.
evidence: They caused it to be as a craved treasure of mythology
He plunged like a mad horse at it.

questions.prompt: How does Crane describe the rival color bearer? Why give the enemy’s flag-bearer so much attention?
facilitatorNotes: He is “bitten vitally,” fights “as with invisible ghouls fastened greedily upon his limbs,” and hugs “his precious flag” with a “terrible grin of resolution,” trying to carry it to safety. He shows the same devotion Henry feels for his own flag. Wilson, not Henry, seizes it “as a panther at prey” while the man dies; “There was much blood upon the grass blades” deflates the triumph.
evidence: With this terrible grin of resolution he hugged his precious flag to him
There was much blood upon the grass blades.

questions.prompt: The four prisoners each react differently. Which one does Henry study most closely, and why might that be?
facilitatorNotes: The last, silent one, on whom “Shame was upon him”: shame at capture and regret for “the right to antagonize.” Henry knows private shame well, and may see himself. Others may point to the boy who talks easily with his captors, as if the two sides share one experience: “voices from where all had been darkness and speculation.” Either answer needs the text.
evidence: Shame was upon him
It seemed a great satisfaction to hear voices from where all had been darkness and speculation.

readings.title: The Red Badge of Courage: a quiet manhood (Chapter XXIV)
readings.challenge: Weigh Henry’s final judgment of himself against what the novel has shown, and decide how far the narrator shares it.
readings.focus: The novel’s ending: memory sorted into public glory and private shame, and a peace Henry may claim too easily.
readings.context: Recap: in a last charge the regiment drove the gray soldiers from a rail fence; Wilson captured their flag, and four prisoners were taken. Henry and Wilson sat side by side and congratulated each other. Earlier, Henry ran from his first fight; wandering among the wounded, he walked beside a tattered soldier who kindly asked where he was hurt, and then left that dying man alone in a field. Later a blow to the head gave Henry the wound his comrades took for a bullet wound. “I swan” is a mild oath; Hasbrouck is the lieutenant.
readings.contentNote: These war-fiction excerpts contain battlefield violence, death, injury and profanity. The narrative critically examines heroic expectations and a frightened soldier’s self-justifications. Henry remembers abandoning a badly wounded man; the soldiers’ talk includes mild profanity.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXIV, the whole chapter, the end of the novel (the printed “THE END.” is left out); opens “The roarings that had stretched in a long line of sound across the face of the forest…”; closes “Over the river a golden ray of sun came through the hosts of leaden rain clouds.”.

questions.prompt: As Henry “struggled to marshal all his acts,” how does he sort them? What does the image of a procession suggest?
facilitatorNotes: His public deeds are “paraded in great and shining prominence,” marching “in wide purple and gold”: memory becomes a parade for an audience. His flight from the first fight is a ghost that “danced.” The deeds others saw shine; the ones no one saw haunt him. Ask what this says about where Henry’s sense of himself comes from.
evidence: his public deeds were paraded in great and shining prominence
the ghost of his flight from the first engagement appeared to him and danced

questions.prompt: Why is the memory of the tattered soldier worse for Henry than the memory of running away?
facilitatorNotes: Running was fear, and many ran; leaving the tattered man was cruelty to someone who had been kind to him, a dying man “deserted in the field.” The narrator calls it “this vision of cruelty.” Yet Henry’s first chill is “at the thought that he might be detected”: is he sorry, or afraid of being found out? Readers will differ; ask for evidence.
evidence: he who, blind with weariness and pain, had been deserted in the field
at the thought that he might be detected in the thing

questions.prompt: What do the scraps of the soldiers’ talk add to the ending?
facilitatorNotes: They cannot even agree on whether they were beaten (“a durn good lickin'” or “We ain't licked, sonny”); someone praises Hasbrouck; someone tells another to shut up. Each man has his own version of the battle, as Henry has his. Their plain talk sits against Henry’s grand reflections.
evidence: I'd say we got a durn good lickin'.
We ain't licked, sonny.

questions.prompt: “He was a man.” “Scars faded as flowers.” Does the ending support Henry’s conclusion, or question it?
facilitatorNotes: Henry “mustered force to put the sin at a distance”: he does not repair it, he sets it aside. The prose rises (“hot plowshares to prospects of clover”) while the march goes on in rain and mud, and “many discovered” the world “to be made of oaths and walking sticks.” The golden ray can be read as real peace or as one more grand image Henry has not earned. Both readings are defensible; the strongest answers quote the last three paragraphs.
evidence: Yet gradually he mustered force to put the sin at a distance.
Over the river a golden ray of sun came through the hosts of leaden rain clouds.
